unit.title: The strategy desk
unit.summary: Undercuts, safety-car calls, offsets and reading the race as a strategist.

lessons.title: Stints and pit windows
lessons.objective: Build a two-stint plan and find its pit window.

payload.prompt: What is a stint in F1?

options.text: A stretch of the race on one set of tyres from stop to stop.
options.explanation: Right. A stint ends when you pit for fresh tyres.

options.text: One lap of the circuit.
options.explanation: No, a stint is multiple laps. It runs from one pit stop to the next.

options.text: A penalty where a driver is slowed for a violation.
options.explanation: That is not a stint. A stint is a period on one set of tyres.

options.text: The time it takes a pit crew to change all four tyres.
options.explanation: That is a pit stop, not a stint. A stint is the racing between stops.

explanation.correct: Right. A stint is a stretch of the race on one tyre set, from one pit stop to the next.
explanation.incorrect: A stint is a racing period on a single set of tyres. Most races have two or three stints.
explanation.sayThisLine: A stint is one set of tyres, from stop to stop.

payload.prompt: What is a pit window?

options.text: The range of laps where a pit stop makes sense based on tyre life and track position.
options.explanation: Right. A pit window opens when tyres are worn and close when rivals pit.

options.text: The time it takes to drive through the pit lane.
options.explanation: That is pit time loss, not a pit window. A window is a range of laps.

options.text: A rule that says you must pit at a certain point in the race.
options.explanation: There is no such rule. Pit windows are strategy-based, not mandatory.

options.text: The number of pit boxes available to a team.
options.explanation: That is pit box availability. A pit window is a strategic timing window.

explanation.correct: Right. A pit window is the strategic range of laps where stopping gains time or holds position.
explanation.incorrect: A pit window is the range of laps where a pit stop is optimal, based on tyre wear and rival strategies.
explanation.sayThisLine: A pit window is a strategic range of laps for pitting.

payload.prompt: Match stint concepts to their definitions.

pairs.definition: A stretch of racing on one set of tyres, from pit stop to pit stop.
The range of laps where a pit stop makes strategic sense.
A race run with only a single pit stop.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty issued by the FIA.
A rule that applies only to the top three teams.

explanation.sayThisLine: Strategy is about timing, pit windows and tyre management.

lessons.title: The undercut in detail
lessons.objective: Predict when an undercut works and when it fails.

payload.prompt: Does the undercut work here?

explanation.correct: The undercut works when you pit earlier and gain track position via a better tyre.
explanation.incorrect: You need fresh tyres to make up the pit loss. Pitting early is the undercut strategy.
explanation.sayThisLine: Fresh tyres undercut a rival's track position.

payload.prompt: Is pit loss about 20–25 seconds?

choices.label: Yes, pit loss is 20–25 seconds total.
No, modern stops are under 10 seconds.

explanation.correct: Pit loss includes speed limit, stop time, and acceleration back to racing pace.
explanation.incorrect: The stop itself is 2 seconds, but total pit loss is 20–25 seconds.
explanation.sayThisLine: Pit loss is 20–25 seconds: limit, stop time, acceleration.

payload.prompt: Should you try an overcut here?

choices.label: Yes, stay out and pass later.

explanation.correct: The overcut is staying out, letting them pit first, then pitting to new tyres and passing.
explanation.incorrect: Pitting first gives them the chance to overcut you. Patience is the overcut.
explanation.sayThisLine: Overcut: patience beats speed early, tyres late.

lessons.title: Managing tyres and lifting off
lessons.objective: Explain lift and coast and tyre saving as a strategy.

payload.prompt: On a hard tyre at a high-speed circuit, roughly how many laps of full-speed racing until grip starts to collapse?

explanation.correct: Right. Hard tyres can last around 35 laps at pace before hitting the cliff.
explanation.incorrect: Hard-compound tyres typically last 30-40 laps at racing pace before grip drops sharply.
explanation.sayThisLine: Hard tyres last roughly 35 laps; softs, around 20.

payload.prompt: Lift and coast saves how many tenths per lap on average?

explanation.correct: Right. Lift and coast costs about 0.3 tenths per lap but saves significant tyre or energy.
explanation.incorrect: Lift and coast typically costs 0.2 to 0.4 tenths per lap but extends tyre life or battery charge.
explanation.sayThisLine: Lift and coast costs about 0.3 tenths but saves more later.

payload.prompt: Should you save the tyres or push to build a gap?

situation.narrative: You are leading by two seconds with 10 laps to go. Your tyres are graining; they will not last at full pace.

options.label: Save and manage
options.consequence: You extend tyre life and keep the lead by managing pace. Risk: you stay vulnerable if he finds extra pace.
considerations: Graining tyres often hit a sudden cliff
A cliff collapse at lap 8 could lose you the lead in one lap
Saving extends life predictably

options.label: Push hard to build a bigger buffer
options.consequence: You risk accelerating tyre cliff, potentially losing more than your 2-second cushion.
considerations: Pushing now feels like winning, but tyres are fragile
If they fail suddenly, the leader closes in seconds
Better to guarantee a safe finish than gamble on dodging the cliff

payload.expertNote: When a tyre is in danger (graining or blistering), extend its life. A guaranteed finish beats a risky collapse.
payload.sayThisLine: Manage the tyres; the lead is safe if you finish.

payload.prompt: Do you lift and coast or keep pushing?

situation.narrative: You have a 1.2-second lead with 8 laps to go. Your rear tyres are blistering; they could fail suddenly.

options.label: Lift and coast to cool the tyres
options.consequence: You lose about 0.3 seconds per lap but keep the tyres alive. Finishing is guaranteed.
considerations: A rear puncture costs you the race instantly
0.3 sec/lap loss is much smaller than a DNF
Margin shrinks from 1.2 to ~0.6 over 8 laps, still safe

options.label: Keep pushing to build a bigger buffer
options.consequence: Tyres may fail suddenly, costing you the race and points.
considerations: Blistering tyres are on borrowed time
One sudden puncture and the lead vanishes
Not worth the risk with 8 laps to go

payload.expertNote: When a tyre is in danger, lift and coast to extend its life. A guaranteed finish beats a risky collapse.
payload.sayThisLine: Lift and coast to save the tyre; finishing is the win.

payload.prompt: What does tyre saving mean as a strategy?

options.text: Driving smoothly and using lift-and-coast to extend tyre life, sometimes at the cost of lap time.
options.explanation: Right. Tyre saving trades immediate pace for tyre longevity.

options.text: Staying in the pit box and not racing at all.
options.explanation: That is not tyre saving. Tyre saving is about how you drive to extend life.

options.text: Using only soft compounds so tyres last longer.
options.explanation: Softs degrade faster, not slower. Saving is about smooth driving, not tyre choice.

options.text: Pitting twice to use fresh tyres both times.
options.explanation: Extra stops cost pit loss. Tyre saving means fewer stops.

explanation.correct: Right. Tyre saving is smooth driving to extend life. It costs lap time but lets you race longer.
explanation.incorrect: Tyre saving is a strategy of smooth, efficient driving to make tyres last longer in the race.
explanation.sayThisLine: Tyre saving is smooth driving to extend life.

lessons.title: Safety car: the free stop
lessons.objective: Explain why a stop under the safety car is cheap.

payload.prompt: Why is a pit stop under the safety car considered a 'free stop'?

options.text: The field is bunched and slowed, so the pit car loses less time to rivals while stopped.
options.explanation: Right. Everyone is on a parade lap at low speed, so stopping does not cost as much gap time.

options.text: The FIA pays for the pit crew's work.
options.explanation: No, the pit stop is not free in money. It is free in time relative to racing pace.

options.text: You do not lose any time; the stop is instant.
options.explanation: The stop still takes time, but pit loss is smaller because everyone is slowed by the safety car.

options.text: Only one team can pit under a safety car.
options.explanation: Multiple teams can pit. The advantage is the reduced speed makes pit loss less costly.

explanation.correct: Right. A safety-car stop is cheap because the whole field crawls at low speed; your stop time loss is small.
explanation.incorrect: A safety-car stop feels free because pit loss is minimal: the field is bunched and moving slowly.
explanation.sayThisLine: Safety-car stops are cheap because the whole field is bunched and slow.

payload.prompt: When the safety car is out and you pit, who gains the most advantage?

options.text: A driver who is trailing by several seconds, who can pit and rejoin without losing more ground.
options.explanation: Right. A trailing driver can close gaps under the safety car by pitting for free and then following the field.

options.text: The leader, who pits first and loses nothing.
options.explanation: The leader loses position if the field catches up under the safety car.

options.text: No one gains; all stops are equal under a safety car.
options.explanation: Not true. Trailing drivers gain relative position by pitting under the safety car.

options.text: The team with the fastest pit crew.
options.explanation: All stops take roughly the same time. The advantage is for trailing drivers, not crew speed.

explanation.correct: Right. A trailing driver benefits most: pit under the safety car, then join the field without losing further ground.
explanation.incorrect: A safety-car stop is most valuable for trailing drivers, who can pit and keep pace with the field.
explanation.sayThisLine: Trailing drivers gain most from a safety-car stop.

payload.prompt: Match pit-stop concepts to their definitions.

pairs.definition: A pit stop under a yellow/safety-car period when pit loss is minimal.
The time cost of driving through the pit lane: roughly 20 seconds.
Both team cars pitting in consecutive laps to optimize strategy.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty issued by the FIA.
A rule that applies only to the top three teams.

explanation.sayThisLine: Strategy is about timing, pit windows and tyre management.

lessons.title: Safety car: pit or stay out?
lessons.objective: Make the call in messy situations and defend it.

payload.prompt: Pit under the VSC or stay out?

situation.narrative: A virtual safety car is deployed. You are third, 0.8 seconds behind the leader. Your tyres have only 5 laps of life.

options.label: Pit for fresh tyres under the VSC
options.consequence: You pit with reduced pit loss (VSC lowers speed delta). Fresh tyres and a chance to jump ahead.
considerations: VSC reduces pit-loss advantage
Fresh tyres after 5 laps of life are much faster
You could emerge in a better position

options.label: Stay out and keep position
options.consequence: You keep P3 but tyres will die soon. The advantage fades as grip collapses.
considerations: Staying avoids pit loss in absolute terms
But tyre cliff is imminent; you will lose positions anyway
Pitting now is the smarter long-term strategy

payload.expertNote: Under a VSC, pit loss is reduced but not zero. Pitting for fresh tyres is often the right call.
payload.sayThisLine: VSC pit stops are cheaper than normal; consider fresh tyres.

payload.prompt: Do you pit or stay out as the leader?

situation.narrative: You lead by 1.5 seconds. A safety car is deployed and the field bunches. Your strategist radios the pit call.

options.label: Stay out and keep the lead
options.consequence: You keep P1. The field catches up under the SC but you restart ahead.
considerations: As leader, staying out is safest
The field closes but you restart on the front row
Pitting risks losing the lead to the bunch

options.label: Pit for fresh tyres
options.consequence: You pit and rejoin in traffic. The field is closer on the restart.
considerations: Fresh tyres help on the restart
But you rejoin in the middle of the pack
Losing track position as the leader is risky

payload.expertNote: As the leader under a safety car, usually stay out. Your track position is valuable.
payload.sayThisLine: Leaders usually stay out under a safety car to keep position.

payload.prompt: Match safety-car concepts to their definitions.

pairs.definition: Everyone slows to a delta time without a physical pace car; gaps stay the same.
Where you run on the road; crucial when passing is hard.
A pit stop during a safety car where time loss is small.

distractorDefinitions: A penalty issued by the FIA.
A rule that applies only to the top three teams.

explanation.sayThisLine: Strategy is about timing, pit windows and tyre management.

lessons.title: Offset strategies
lessons.objective: Explain why teams start on different tyres.

payload.prompt: Start on softs or mediums for P2?

situation.narrative: Qualifying is done. P1 starts on soft tyres (fastest). You are P2. You must decide your race start compound: soft (matching P1) or medium (offset for a later stop).

options.label: Start on soft tyres to match P1.
options.consequence: You both pit around the same time. Similar track position throughout.
considerations: Matches your rival's strategy
No pit-window advantage
Consistent race but no strategic edge

options.label: Start on mediums (offset strategy).
options.consequence: You pit 10+ laps later. Fresh tyres give you track advantage after P1 pits.
considerations: Opens a different pit window
Fresh tyres can pass them after their stop
Offset strategy is about timing, not pace

payload.expertNote: Offset strategy means different starting compounds to pit at different times and gain track position.
payload.sayThisLine: Offset: start different to pit different and gain track position.

payload.prompt: What is the main benefit of an offset strategy?

options.text: Different starting tyres create different pit windows, so one team may undercut or overcut the other.
options.explanation: Right. Offset opens two separate windows instead of copying your rival.

options.text: Starting on a soft tyre means you will never pit.
options.explanation: No, softs degrade fast and force an early stop.

options.text: Offset strategies are only used by backmarker teams.
options.explanation: No, any team can use an offset to avoid a crowded pit window.

options.text: It guarantees that you will lead the race at some point.
options.explanation: An offset creates strategy variety, but does not guarantee a lead.

explanation.correct: Right. An offset strategy forces rivals to pit at different times, opening opportunities to undercut or gain position.
explanation.incorrect: An offset strategy is starting on a different tyre compound to create a separate pit window.
explanation.sayThisLine: Offset strategies avoid matching your rival's pit window.

payload.prompt: Risk traffic or extend tyres to avoid it?

situation.narrative: You are in the undercut pit window. P1 has not pitted yet. Pit now and risk getting held up by backmarkers. Stay out 3 more laps and avoid traffic but lose tyre life.

options.label: Pit now for the undercut.
options.consequence: You pit with fresh tyres and gain track position despite traffic.
considerations: Undercut timing is critical
Traffic delays are usually small
Fresh tyres more valuable than avoiding traffic

options.label: Extend 3 more laps to avoid traffic.
options.consequence: Tyres degrade. P1 pits while you are still out. You lose the undercut advantage.
considerations: Pit loss overrides short traffic delays
Tyres degrade fast on worn compound
You give up the undercut window

payload.expertNote: Undercut pit windows are tight. Traffic delays matter less than tyre advantage.
payload.sayThisLine: Undercut timing beats avoiding traffic. Pit when tyres say so.

payload.prompt: In an offset strategy, what is a common tyre-choice scenario?

options.text: One car starts on softs, another on mediums, so they pit at different laps and open separate strategies.
options.explanation: Right. This is a classic offset: softs pit earlier, mediums pit later.

options.text: Both cars start on the same tyre to be fair.
options.explanation: That is the opposite of an offset. An offset means different tyres.

options.text: Starting on hards to guarantee you do not pit.
options.explanation: Even hards require a stop in most races. Offset is about pit-window separation.

options.text: Starting on wets even when the track is dry.
options.explanation: That would be a tactical error, not an offset strategy.

explanation.correct: Right. A typical offset: soft-tyre car pits around lap 15-18, medium-tyre car around lap 22-25.
explanation.incorrect: A common offset: one car on softs for early pit, one on mediums for a later pit window.
explanation.sayThisLine: Soft-vs-medium offset opens two pit windows.

lessons.title: Weather and the crossover
lessons.objective: Decide when to switch tyres as a track dries.

payload.prompt: Switch now or wait until P1 pits?

situation.narrative: Rain is getting heavier. You are on intermediates, P1 is also on inters and is 0.6 seconds ahead. Both of you could switch to wets soon. Do you switch now or wait to see if P1 pits first?

options.label: Switch to wets now, gain the initiative.
options.consequence: You pit first with fresh wets. Pit loss is your only cost; you regain pace quickly.
considerations: Fresh wets give immediate grip gain
P1 must react to your pit
Being first means you set the pace

options.label: Wait and react when P1 pits.
options.consequence: You both switch at about the same time. P1 has a small head start out of the pits.
considerations: Reduces risk of wrong tyre choice
Gives P1 the pit initiative
You follow, not lead

payload.expertNote: Tyre-switch timing is a gamble. Being first gives you freshness; reacting gives information.
payload.sayThisLine: Switch early for pace, late for info. Choose your risk.

payload.prompt: At what lap does full-wet tyre become faster than intermediate?

explanation.correct: Around lap 8, wets are faster than inters in heavy rain. Crossover depends on rain intensity.
explanation.incorrect: Crossover varies by rain rate. In heavy rain, wets catch up by lap 8–10.
explanation.sayThisLine: Rain-tyre crossover is around lap 8 in heavy conditions.

payload.prompt: Switch to full wets or stay on inters?

situation.narrative: Rain is intensifying. Standing water is forming on corners. You are on intermediate tyres. Your team radios that full wets are ready and available.

options.label: Pit for full wets now.
options.consequence: Full wets grip the water. Lower aquaplane risk, better pace in standing water.
considerations: Full wets are built for standing water
Aquaplane is dangerous and unpredictable
Pit loss is worth the safety and grip

options.label: Stay on inters; they are still working.
options.consequence: Inters degrade in standing water. Risk of aquaplaning and loss of control.
considerations: In standing water, wets are faster
Aquaplane can cause a crash or DNF
Waiting costs lap time and safety

payload.expertNote: Full wets are for standing water and heavy rain. Inters are for a damp track.
payload.sayThisLine: Wets for standing water, inters for damp. Know the rain.

payload.prompt: What is the crossover point in tyre strategy?

options.text: The lap when the time gain from a new tyre exceeds the cost of pitting, making a stop worthwhile.
options.explanation: Right. The crossover is a calculated point in time.

options.text: A place on the track where the surface changes from wet to dry.
options.explanation: That is a track feature, not a crossover point. Crossover is a strategic timing.

options.text: A rule that says drivers must switch tyres at a specific lap.
options.explanation: There is no such rule. Crossover is a calculation, not a mandate.

options.text: A penalty where tyres are cross-threaded and must be replaced.
options.explanation: That is not a crossover point. Crossover is strategic timing.

explanation.correct: Right. The crossover point is when the new tyre's lap-time advantage equals the pit stop's time cost.
explanation.incorrect: The crossover point is the moment when switching to a new tyre saves time overall versus staying out.
explanation.sayThisLine: Crossover is when the new tyre's gain exceeds pit loss.

payload.prompt: When do you use intermediate tyres instead of full wets?

options.text: When the track is damp but with no standing water, and rain is light or stopping.
options.explanation: Right. Inters are the bridge tyre: wetter than dry, drier than full wets.

options.text: Only in qualifying, not in races.
options.explanation: Inters are used in races during light-rain phases and track-drying periods.

options.text: Never; full wets are always faster in any rain.
options.explanation: No, full wets are slower on a drying or lightly wet track. Inters are faster then.

options.text: When tyre manufacturers run out of full wets.
options.explanation: Tyre availability is not the reason. Inters are chosen by track conditions.

explanation.correct: Right. Inters are for damp tracks and light rain. Full wets are for heavy rain and standing water.
explanation.incorrect: Intermediate tyres are used for damp tracks and light-to-moderate rain without standing water.
explanation.sayThisLine: Inters for damp, wets for standing water.

lessons.title: From qualifying to race plan
lessons.objective: Explain how track evolution and grid slot shape the plan.

payload.prompt: Does a cooler race day change your strategy from qualifying?

situation.narrative: You qualified on pole at 1:23.5. The race is tomorrow on a cooler day. Forecast suggests the track will be 0.3-0.5 seconds slower.

options.label: Adjust pit strategy for the cooler track
options.consequence: You re-plan pit windows and tyre wear. Slower track = slower tyre degradation = later pits.
considerations: Track evolution changes grip and degradation rates
Cooler = slower tyre wear = longer stint life
Pit windows shift 2-3 laps later

options.label: Stick to the qualifying-day strategy
options.consequence: You follow the plan, but pit windows may not align with actual tyre wear.
considerations: Pole position gives you an advantage
But tyre degradation changes with grip; you will be off pace
Strategy must adapt to track conditions

payload.expertNote: Track conditions change how tyres wear. Race strategy adapts from qualifying.
payload.sayThisLine: Cooler track = slower laps = slower tyre wear = later pit windows.

payload.prompt: How does track evolution affect pit windows?

situation.narrative: A slow track evolves less during the race. Rubber lays down slowly, grip builds gradually. Lap times improve only slightly through the race.

facts.label: Tyre degradation rate
facts.value: Slower than on a fast track

options.label: Pit windows open later on a slow track
options.consequence: You stay out longer, tyres last longer, pit later. Tyre wear is slower on a slow track.
considerations: Slow track = lower grip = slower lap times = slower tyre wear
Tyres live longer, so windows open 2-3 laps later
Fast track is the opposite: windows open earlier

options.label: Pit windows stay the same as on a fast track
options.consequence: You pit too early. Tyres still have life, and you lose the undercut opportunity.
considerations: Track speed directly affects tyre wear
A one-size-fits-all strategy does not account for grip
You will be off pace compared to rivals who adapt

payload.expertNote: Track evolution and grip affect tyre wear. Slow track = slower degradation = later pit windows.
payload.sayThisLine: Slow track, later pits. Fast track, earlier pits. Adapt to grip.

pairs.definition: The track gets faster as rubber lays down and grip builds during a weekend.
The order cars line up in for the start, set by qualifying plus any penalties.
Starting on a different tyre from rivals to open a different pit window.

A rule that applies only to the top three teams.

explanation.sayThisLine: Strategy is about timing, pit windows and tyre management.
